_about: The history dial (Version 70, the grand campaign). One setting, chosen when a campaign starts and open to change in any month: how far the war the computer runs may move away from the war that was fought. It leashes the computer-run world and never the player. Stop 3 is the game with nothing added, and a campaign with no stop stored is played at it. 'stops' are the five stops: 'mood' multiplies how far a staff's nerve differs from one war to the next (open.json 'mood'); 'lean' says how a staff's character is dealt: 'real' gives each nation the character its staff most often has (rivals.json 'lean'), a number flattens the national lean toward an even deal (0 the lean as it stands, 1 an even deal); 'other' multiplies the monthly chance of a great choice history never took ('unhistoric'); 'league' multiplies the chance that small countries found a League unprovoked or join one; 'join' is the monthly chance that a neutral whose opinion has reached the mark joins a bloc it never joined in history (1 where nothing holds it back; 'joined' lists who really did, and a neutral the player has courted is his affair at every stop); 'early' is how many months before its usual first month a great choice may be taken up. At a stop with 'book' the great choices keep history's calendar: one with a date in 'dates' (months of the war, 1 for September 1939) is taken up so that the blow falls in that month, give or take 'slack' months by the war's seed, with no monthly draw and no postponement, and on odds as short as 'nerve' times what its staff would usually ask; one that followed another nation into a war (no date, not unhistoric) follows at once. The book yields when it no longer fits. Each choice belongs to a 'theatre', and 'marks' are what history's calendar expects there: the 'if' list (as in diplomacy.json, with 'a|b' for either) must hold in every month before 'until', or from the month after 'by' on, the slack allowed. When a mark fails the book is closed in that theatre and in every theatre that comes 'after' it: from then on the staffs there decide as at stop 3, and the news says so. A theatre with 'stays' is the exception (b530): at its stops, while the month is no later than its 'by', it does not close with one it comes after but waits; it stands once its 'if' holds, and closes with its own 'why' when 'by' is past without it. 'shores' are the book's word on the second front (theatre 'second'): while it stands no computer staff lands an army from the sea on the home ground of the 'owners' before the month 'from' (the slack allowed; '*' is every other shore, overseas ground included): North Africa from November 1942, Italy from July 1943, France and the north from June 1944, the British Isles never. A shore with 'islands' named and a 'mainland' month keeps the islands' month under 'from' and opens its mainland in the later one (ruling 233(a): Sicily and Sardinia from July 1943, the Italian mainland from September). 'usual' is the shore's month in the usual game (ruling 233(b)): at the stops where history's dates hold and no book stands on the second front (stop 3, and a stop with a book once it is closed there), no computer staff lands on the owners' home ground, islands included, before it (Italy: April 1943). 'facing' names the far shore opposite (ruling 233(e)): by the book and in the usual game alike nobody lands on the owners' home ground while anyone on their side holds one of those provinces or has a corps there, whoever's flag flies over it (Italy: no landing while an Axis army holds Tunis, Sfax or Mareth; a neutral there is no bar). That is a rule for the first crossing: it is spent for as long as an enemy of the owner stands on its home ground. By the book the march over a strait from an island named to the mainland is a crossing too, and no computer staff makes it before the mainland's month (ruling 233(i)). Colonies are open as before, the two loosest stops leave it to the staff, and a player lands and marches when he likes. 'ambitions' are claims on named ground, read at the stops that have 'ambitions': a computer-run country ('nat') with a claim on ground another ('on') holds presses it when the holder is weakened ('weak': at war, and either its will to fight is down to that share or the claimant's strength against what stands near the claim is 'odds' or better; ground reached only by sea counts as weakly held with no more than 'thin' divisions on it), and at a stop marked 'bold' whenever the odds are that good, at war or not, once the claimant has bided its time (up to 'wait' months, by the war's seed); at a stop with 'share' only that share of the claims is alive in any one war, dealt from its seed. Pressing is a warning: the news and the Powers tab say so. A great power of the holder's alliance that stands on the claimant's own border deters it until that power has itself lost 'guard' of its will to fight (not asked at a bold stop). After 'notice' months, if the holder is still weak, it marches with chance 'chance' a month, and the news gives the reason. A warning that has gone 'lapse' months without the conditions holding is dropped. A claimant that marches on a member of one alliance fights beside the other as a co-belligerent if that alliance is at war with the holder; each month a great power of the holder's alliance that borders the claimant stands by its ally with chance 'aid'. A war between two countries outside both alliances ends when the claimant has held all the ground it claims for 'treaty' months (1: the first month it is found holding it all): the ground is its own by treaty and the two are at peace. An ambition with 'stop' is read only from that stop up; one with 'if' only when those conditions hold; 'lift' is the shipping the claimant gathers when it marches on ground across the sea. At a stop with 'deal' every neutral's leaning between the alliances is dealt afresh from the war's seed within 'deal' points either way, and the news names those who have changed their minds.

stops.name: By the book
stops.blurb: The computer keeps to the war that was fought for as long as the war still looks like it.
lines: The great attacks fall in history's months: Norway in April 1940, the west in May, the east in June 1941.
Only the countries that really joined the war join it, each on its real side.

No second front before its time: North Africa from November 1942, Italy from July 1943, France from June 1944. So Germany has longer before it must fight in the west, and the Soviet Union fights alone for longer.
Every general staff has the character its real counterpart had.
Where you leave the book, the book is closed: the staffs there think for themselves from then on.

stops.name: Close to history
stops.blurb: History's war with the dates loosened: each great attack falls within a season of its real month.
lines: The great attacks fall within a month or so of history's dates, and you cannot be sure which.
A country that stayed out of the real war seldom joins this one.

The Allies open no second front before history's dates: North Africa from November 1942, Italy from July 1943, France from June 1944. So Germany has longer before it must fight in the west, and the Soviet Union fights alone for longer.
The general staffs have their real characters, with a little nerve of their own.
Where you leave the book, the book is closed.

stops.name: History's shape
stops.blurb: The war starts as it did and nobody follows the book after that. Staffs attack when they like their chances.
lines: Each staff decides for itself when to strike, so the west may open in March or wait for 1941.

The western Allies' staffs keep history's order for their great landings: the Italian mainland from July 1943, France from May 1944, or sooner once Germany itself is invaded. Islands and colonies at any time, and you land when you like.
Neutrals drift with the fortunes of war and can be courted.
The character of each staff is dealt afresh every war, with a national lean.

stops.name: Loose
stops.blurb: History's shape, and neutrals with ambitions of their own: a weakened neighbour is an opportunity.
lines: Countries with a claim on a neighbour's ground press it when that neighbour is weakened, and may march for it. Which claims are alive differs from war to war.
You can read every claim beforehand on the Powers tab, and the news warns you before anyone marches.
Staffs are less predictable, and choices history never took come up more often: the western Allies no longer wait for history's dates to land in Italy or France.

stops.name: Anything goes
stops.blurb: Nobody has read the history books. Any country may pick either side, or go for a neighbour on its own account.
lines: Every neutral's leaning is dealt afresh: Spain may side with the Allies, Turkey with the Axis.
Claims are pressed whenever the odds look good, between neutrals too.
The great attacks may come months earlier, and any staff may have any character.

bookIf._note: By the book a dated choice is taken when these hold, in place of its own conditions (open.json): history's month is the staff's reason, and what was a precondition in the real war may already be over in this one. Italy came in as France was falling: with France already fallen in her month she comes in all the same. Germany went into the Balkans while Italy was held in Greece: with Greece already beaten she goes for Yugoslavia in her month all the same.

stays._note: b530: the east's book hangs on France's fall by the east's own month, not on the west's mark. At stops 1 and 2, when the west's book closes, the east's waits: it stands once France is out of the war with Germany and the Soviet Union still at peace, and closes when May 1941 (turn 21) is over without that.
stays.why: France was still in the war when May 1941 ended
stays.ask: France is still in the war

marks.why: Norway is at war before its time
the war in the west has not waited for the spring of 1940
Germany has not struck in the west
Italy is at war before its time
Italy has stayed out of the war
the Balkans are at war before their time
Germany has left the Balkans alone
Germany and the Soviet Union are at war before the summer of 1941
the Soviet Union has left Finland alone

restraint._about: The book's restraints (ruling 139, the design director's b509(c) and b512(g, h)): at the stops named, a computer staff keeps to what was chosen in the real war even where its own judgement would go further. 'storm': the towns a computer staff, and any computer ally standing round them with it, rings and does not storm (it may still starve them out). 'enter': the ground a computer staff's armies do not go into, to march or to attack. 'fed': a town held by its own side ('nat') whose stores do not run down while the computer staff named ('by') rings it, with no player beside it. 'front' (b527): the seats on that front; where a player holds any one of them none of the restraints applies, so that a player never faces, or fights beside, a city that cannot fall. A player is never held to any of them, and a player's ring starves the town as any other.

storm.why: in September 1941 Hitler chose to starve Leningrad rather than storm it

enter.why: in 1941 Finland's army halted on the Karelian Isthmus at the frontier of 1939

fed.why: for 872 days Leningrad was fed, barely, across Lake Ladoga: by boat in summer and over the ice road in winter
